text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

The A$10 billion float of Telstra moved ahead yesterday with the Federal Government announcing the team of investment banks that will oversee the share offer. JB Were & Son was named as the Australian agent with ABN Amro Rothschild in Europe and Credit Suisse First Boston in the America. These agents will be joined by several other agents who will act as lead managers. Page 1.

The Australian manufacturing industry remains sluggish despite signs the economy is strengthening. Analysts claim it was the manufacturing sector which contributed to a majority of the 0.2 per cent increase in unemployment to 8.8 per cent for February. Th Australian Bureau of Statistics figures also reveal that job growth since November last year has been weaker than originally predicted. Page 1.

Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan has rejected a strong Australian request to dump mercenaries training anti-rebel forces on Bougainville. Papua New Guinea's defiant stance comes after a meeting between both countries' Prime Ministers in Ausralia last weekend. Page 3.

Pressure is increasing on controversial Independent Senator Mal Colston to resign from the Senate following the Opposition's successful push for his departure from the Australian National University Council and a Senate committee. Colston, alleged to have rorted parliamentary travel allowances, resigned following
Labor's continued criticism of him serving on the university council. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Australia's unemployment rate has risen to its highest point in the past two and a half years. Latest jobless figures have put an end to the run of recent positive economic news with a jump of 0.2 percentage points in February to post Australia's unemploymnt rate at 8.8 per cent. This translates to an increase in the number of jobless by 19,900 to 810,800 in seasonally
adjusted estimates for the period. Page 1.

Australia's battered relationship with Papua New Guinea was plunged into fresh crisis yesterday when the PNG Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan rejected Australia's pleas and announced he would continue with the plan to send mercenaries to Bougainville. Chan' decision follows a meeting with Australian Prime Minister John Howard in Sydney last week, where the leaders discussed alternatives to the mercenary plan. Page 1.

In the wake of recent Australian imitations, it has been revealed that award-winning author Wanda Koolmatrie is not an Aboriginal writer "taken from her parents as a child", but a 47-year-old white man named Leon Carmen from Sydney. Publishing industry reresentatives say the latest cultural hoax signals an "epidemic". Page 1.

Federal Transport Minister John Sharp has ended his campaign to force the resignation of the entire Civil Aviation Safety Authority board. Senior Government sources have confirmed that Sharp will not be moving against the board in the foreseeable
future. This follows Sharp's public threats to sack the entire board last month, claiming there were "good grounds" to do so. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Prime Minister John Howard has promised "faster and stronger" economic growth following figures revealing a surge in unemployment. The February labour force survey by the Australian Bureau of Statistics revealed unemployment is now 28 per cent among those aged 15-19. While the national unemployment rate
rose 0.2 points to 8.8 per cent, figures in NSW jumped from 7.8 per cent to 8.5 per cent. The proportion of the workforce in full-time jobs fell to a two-year low of 74.6 per cent. Page 1.

After 370 days, NSW's most far reaching inquiry - from the way the legal system has been polluted to corrupt police practices, through to revelations of sexual abuse - the Police Royal Commission has finished its public hearings. When the last witness finished at 3.10pm yesterday, Commissioner Justice James Wood said he was sad but also relieved that the hearings had ended and that overall he was happy with what the commission
had achieved. Page 1.

NSW Premier Bob Carr has ordered Education Minister, John Aquilina, to make his department more competent and get better value for money in education. Carr's directions follow revelations in the Police Royal Commission which uncovered departmental protecton for teachers accused of sexual misconduct against students, and claims by the department's senior bureaucrats that they were unaware of the extent of protection. Page 1.

At an emergency meeting in Melbourne yesterday State and Territory Attorney-Generals have set the scene for a legal aid showdown with the Federal Government. The States will insist the Commonwealth slash more public servants instead of slashing legal aid unds to meet its Budget targets. Federal Attorney-General Daryl Williams will meet with the States today to discuss a plan to cut legal aid spending by more than A$120 million. Page 2.
THE AGE

Victoria took a double hit on the jobs front yesterday, with Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showing that the unemployment rate climbed to nine per cent last month and a study revealing that Victoria has up to five regions with youth unemployment bove 20 per cent. In terms of job creation, Victoria did better than most states, with 31,400 new jobs created in the past year - the highest figure of any State. Page A1.

Family Court head Justice Alastair Nicholson has spoken out against cuts to legal aid, saying unrepresented people in court makes a "mockery" of laws protecting domestic-violence victims. At a conference organised by the Victorian Court Network, Justice Ncholson said proposals to cut legal aid funding by A$120 million over three years had already increased the risk of Family Court judges making faulty decisions. Page A1.

Former Labor Prime Minister Gough Whitlam has attacked the Australian Labor Party for proposing a moratorium on tariff cuts in the car industry. While slamming the protection policies of the 1930s and 1960s under conservative Governments, Whitlam accused the Opposition of regional populism and "not even good politics". Page A2.

The battle to protect the glass-mosaic ceiling of the National Gallery of Victoria has intensified, with the National Trust accusing Gallery management of being arrogant and secretive about its renovation plans. The gallery is planning to
relocate the great hall's ceiling as part of a A$160 million redevelopment. Page A1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
